Antilymphocyte immunoglobulins or muromonab- CD3 may be used for severe or corticosteroid-unrespon- sive episodes.1,2,7,9,13,15 Azathioprine, sirolimus, or myco- phenolate mofetil have also been used adjunctively for treatment of rejection,1,7 although concerns persist about the use of mycophenolate in intestinal transplantation (see above). Chronic rejection, a common cause of late graft dysfunction, is more difficult to treat.1,9,16 Infliximab has been tried.17 Bacterial, viral, and fungal infections are also common post-transplant,1,2,9,16 and may be confused with rejec- tion.4,16 Protocols for antimicrobial prophylaxis and treat- ment are similar to those used for other solid organ trans- plants. Selective gastrointestinal decontamination with non-absorbable oral antibacterials is usually performed during the first fortnight after transplantation, and during moderate to severe rejection episodes.10,11 The high level of immunosuppression necessary in intestinal transplanta- tion makes recipients particularly susceptible to post- transplant lymphoproliferative disease associated with Ep- stein-Barr virus infection.1,2,4,6,16 Controlling rejection by more potent immunosuppression is difficult because of these complications, so the induction of immune tolerance through adjunctive bone marrow infusion is being investi- gated.1,2,12,14 Graft-versus-host disease (see Haematopoi- etic Stem Cell Transplantation, p.1811) may occur and there may be a recurrence of the original disease.2 1.
